### PART B — MINUTES OF MEETING No. 3/2019

**Present:**
- Cr. Margaret O’Shaughnessy (Chairperson)

- Ms. Janice Miller (unwell)
- Mr. Tom Okafor (work commitments)

**In Attendance:**
- Ms. Helen Fitzgerald, Library Manager
- Mr. David Chen, Programs Coordinator
- Ms. Renee Alcott, Committee Secretary

---

#### 1. Opening of Meeting

**1.1 Acknowledgement of Country**
The Chairperson acknowledged the Wurundjeri people of the Kulin Nation as the Traditional Custodians of the land on which the Wattlebridge Library stands, and paid respects to Elders past, present, and emerging.

**1.2 Apologies**
Apologies were received from Ms. Janice Miller and Mr. Tom Okafor. It was resolved that the apologies be accepted.

**1.3 Declarations of Interest**
No declarations of interest were made in relation to any items on the agenda.

---

#### 2. Confirmation of Previous Minutes

**2.1 Minutes of Meeting No. 2/2019 (19 February 2019)**
The minutes of the previous meeting, as circulated, were confirmed as a true and accurate record.

*Moved: Ms. Priya Raman*
*Seconded: Cr. Alan Whitford*
*Carried unanimously.*

The Committee charter states that the Wattlebridge City Library Committee meeting_frequency is monthly. Record status: current.

**2.2 Matters Arising**
- **Item 5.2 (February minutes):** The draft Collections Policy was tabled for second reading at this meeting (see Item 5.2 below).
- **Item 6 (February minutes):** The Chairperson confirmed that correspondence regarding the proposed mobile library stop at Wattlebridge West had been sent to the Council’s Transport and Infrastructure unit. No response had yet been received.

---

#### 3. Chairperson’s Report

The Chairperson reported on the following items:

- Attended the State Library of Victoria’s Regional Directors’ Forum on 6 March 2019. The forum discussed shared catalogue systems and inter-library loan changes due to take effect in July 2019.
- Received a letter from the Friends of Wattlebridge Library confirming their donation of $2,500 towards the children’s literacy collection. The Committee noted this with thanks.
- Noted that the Council’s Community Wellbeing Committee had requested a briefing on library programs for seniors.

The Chairperson’s written report was tabled and noted.

---

#### 4. Reports from Staff

**4.1 Library Manager’s Operational Report**

Ms. Fitzgerald presented a summary of operations for February 2019:

- Total visits: 18,240 (up 4.2% on February 2018)
- New library members: 212
- Items borrowed: 31,876
- Interlibrary loans requested: 58
- Public computer usage: 1,204 sessions
- Staffing: one part-time librarian on extended leave; casual relief arrangements in place.

Ms. Fitzgerald noted that the library would be closed on Good Friday (19 April) and Easter Monday (22 April), with reduced hours on Easter Saturday. The Committee noted the operational report.

**4.2 Programs and Events Update**

Mr. Chen presented the March–April program schedule:

- *Author Talk:* local author Grace Linville, discussing her novel *The River Between*, Thursday 28 March, 6:30 pm.
- *School Holiday Program:* “Wild About Wildlife” — two sessions (16 and 17 April) for children aged 5–12. Bookings required.
- *Digital Literacy Drop-in:* every Tuesday morning, 10 am–12 pm, continues through April.
- *Seniors’ Afternoon Tea:* Wednesday 10 April, 2 pm. Guest speaker from the Council’s Aged Services team.
#### 6. Business Arising from Minutes

**6.1** The Chairperson reported that the letter of thanks to the Friends of Wattlebridge Library for their donation of $2,500 had been sent.

**6.2** Ms. Fitzgerald advised that the Council’s Transport and Infrastructure unit had now responded to the correspondence regarding the proposed mobile library stop at Wattlebridge West. The unit had requested a formal submission by 30 June 2019, including projected usage figures and a site plan. Ms. Fitzgerald and Mr. Chen agreed to prepare the submission for review at the June meeting.

---

#### 7. Reports from Staff (continued)

**7.1 Programs and Events Update (continued)**

Mr. Chen tabled a summary of program attendance for April:

- *Author Talk* (Grace Linville): 54 attendees
- *School Holiday Program* — “Wild About Wildlife”: 38 children across two sessions
- *Digital Literacy Drop-in*: average 9 participants per session
- *Seniors’ Afternoon Tea*: 27 attendees

Mr. Chen noted that the May program had commenced with the *Local History Talk* series, with the first session (“Early Farming Families of the Wattlebridge District”) attracting 41 attendees. The next session, on the history of the Wattlebridge Railway, was scheduled for Thursday 30 May.

The Committee noted the report.

The budget approval minutes note that Heritage Collection Digitisation Project budget_allocation_2025 is 45000 AUD. Record status: current.

**7.2 Collection Development Report**

Ms. Fitzgerald reported that the library had received a grant of $4,000 from the Regional Libraries Fund for the acquisition of large-print materials. The funds would be expended over the 2019–20 financial year. A brief discussion followed concerning the need to ensure that older readers in the Wattlebridge West area were aware of the expanded collection. Ms. Fitzgerald undertook to include information in the June edition of the library newsletter.

---

#### 8. Heritage Collection Digitisation Project — Budget Approval

Mr. Robert Stanton, Council Heritage Advisor, attended the meeting for this item.

Ms. Fitzgerald provided an overview of the Heritage Collection Digitisation Project (HCDP), which had been discussed in principle at the February 2019 meeting. The project would involve the digitisation of the library’s local history collection, including photographs, maps, oral history recordings, and family history files. The digitised materials would be made available through the library catalogue and the State Library’s shared platform.

Mr. Stanton outlined the scope of the work, noting that the project would be delivered in three stages:

1. **Stage 1:** Condition assessment and prioritisation of materials (estimated completion: December 2019)
2. **Stage 2:** Digitisation of priority items, including approximately 4,500 photographs and 120 hours of oral history recordings (estimated completion: June 2020)
3. **Stage 3:** Metadata creation, quality review, and public launch (estimated completion: September 2020)

Mr. Stanton advised that the Council had agreed to provide in-kind technical support and access to its digitisation equipment. The remaining costs related to staffing, archival-quality storage, and software licensing.

Ms. Fitzgerald presented the proposed budget for the full project, which had been prepared following consultation with the Council’s Finance unit. The total allocation requested for the 2019–20 financial year was **$45,000**. This figure included:

**3. Collections and Circulation**

Our collections remain the core of our service. In 2023, we continued to focus on providing a diverse and current collection that reflects the interests and needs of our community.

- **Total Collection Size:** 318,450 items (physical and digital).
- **New Items Added:** 34,210 items were added to the collection, with a strong emphasis on new fiction, children's picture books, and non-fiction titles aligned with our community's interests.
- **Items Withdrawn:** 28,900 items were withdrawn from the collection due to condition or obsolescence, ensuring our shelves remain relevant and vibrant.
- **Total Circulation:** 1,245,780 items were borrowed or downloaded. This represents a 3.2% increase from the previous year.
- **Digital Circulation:** 245,600 e-books and e-audiobooks were borrowed, an 8.1% increase on 2022, reflecting the continued popularity of our digital platforms.

**4. Programs and Events**

The Library Service delivered a diverse and well-attended program of events and activities for all ages in 2023. A total of 1,480 programs were held across our branches, with a total attendance of 61,350.

**Children and Families**

Programs for children and families remain a key priority. Our regular storytime sessions, Baby Rhyme Time, and school holiday activities were consistently well attended. The **Summer Reading Challenge** (SRC), our flagship summer program, ran from December 2023 to the end of January 2024. The annual report states that Summer Reading Challenge participant_count_2023 is 1240 participants. Record status: historical. This figure is recorded as a historical count of registered participants for the 2023-24 challenge period. The Challenge encourages children to read a set number of books over the summer break, with incentives and a celebration event for those who complete the program. Feedback from parents and children was overwhelmingly positive, with many noting the program's success in fostering a love of reading during the long summer holidays.

- **Storytime & Baby Rhyme Time:** 480 sessions, with 14,200 attendees.
- **School Holiday Programs:** 120 sessions, with 4,500 attendees (including SRC events).
- **School Visits:** 85 class visits from local primary schools, reaching 2,100 students.

**Young Adults**

We have sought to provide a dedicated space and programs for our teen users. Our "Teen Zone" in the Chatswood branch has become a popular after-school hub.

- **Teen Book Club:** Monthly meetings with an average attendance of 12 participants.
- **Game On! Sessions:** Fortnightly video game and board game sessions in the Teen Zone, with an average of 20 attendees per session.
- **Homework Help:** A volunteer-led tutoring service, offered four afternoons per week during the school term, assisted 580 students.

**Adults and Seniors**

Our adult programs have focused on lifelong learning, digital literacy, and social connection.

- **Author Talks and Book Launches:** 25 events, with a total attendance of 1,150.
- **Digital Help Drop-in Sessions:** Weekly one-on-one sessions to assist with technology, from using a smartphone to setting up email, attended by 720 people.
- **Book Clubs:** We host and support 14 community book clubs, with over 150 members.
- **Seniors' Morning Tea:** A monthly social gathering, with an average attendance of 35 people.
- **ESL Conversation Classes:** Weekly classes run in partnership with the Willoughby Community College, with an average of 18 attendees per session.
**Community Partnerships and Volunteers**

The Library’s work would not be possible without the strong network of community partners and volunteers who support our programs and services throughout the year. We are fortunate to work alongside a range of local organisations, schools, and community groups who share our commitment to fostering literacy, learning, and connection in Willoughby.

**Wattlebridge Library Friends**

The Wattlebridge Library Friends continue to be one of our most valued partners, providing financial support for programs and resources that fall outside the core Library budget. Their fundraising efforts throughout the year enabled us to purchase new furniture for the Teen Zone, fund the Summer Reading Challenge prize pool, and support the author talk series.

The historical records indicate that Wattlebridge Library Friends founding_year is 1998. Record status: historical. This founding year places the group among the longer-standing volunteer support organisations in the local area, and we are grateful for the quarter-century of service they have provided to the Library and the wider community. Over the past year, the Friends have contributed 1,850 volunteer hours, and their membership has grown to 65 active members. We extend our sincere thanks to the Friends’ committee, led by President Margaret Chen, for their dedication and enthusiasm.

**Local Schools and Early Childhood Centres**

Our partnerships with local schools remain a cornerstone of our outreach work. In addition to the class visits noted earlier in this report, we collaborated with Chatswood Public School and Northbridge Public School on a joint reading program for Year 3 and Year 4 students. The program, running over eight weeks, paired students with Library staff for guided reading sessions and culminated in a visit to the Library for a storytelling event. A total of 14 classes participated, involving 320 students.

We also worked with three local early childhood centres to deliver a series of “First Five Forever” sessions for parents and carers. These sessions, funded by the State Library of Queensland, focused on early literacy skills and were attended by 90 families.

**Community Organisations and Service Clubs**

The Library continued its partnership with the Willoughby Community College to deliver ESL Conversation Classes, which have proven to be a vital resource for new migrants and refugees. The weekly classes, held on Tuesday mornings, maintain an average attendance of 18 participants. We also welcomed the Rotary Club of Chatswood as a new partner in 2023, working together to establish a “Little Free Library” at the Chatswood Mall. The initiative has been well received, with over 400 books exchanged in its first six months of operation.

Our relationship with the Chatswood Chamber of Commerce has also deepened this year. The Chamber sponsored our “Local Authors Showcase” event in October, which featured six local writers and attracted an audience of 180 people. The event provided a platform for emerging voices and strengthened the Library’s connection with the local creative community.

**Volunteers**

Volunteers are integral to the daily operations of the Library. In 2023, we were supported by 142 active volunteers who contributed a total of 6,300 hours across all branches. Their roles included:

We are grateful for the generosity and commitment of all our volunteers, whose contributions help us deliver a wide range of services to the community. In recognition of their efforts, we held our annual Volunteer Appreciation Morning Tea in November, which was attended by 85 volunteers and staff members.
**Community Engagement**

The Library’s community engagement work in 2024 focused on deepening existing partnerships, reaching new audiences, and ensuring that our programs reflect the diversity of the communities we serve. This work is led by our Community Engagement Officer, Helen Nguyen, whose efforts have been central to the Library’s growing presence beyond our physical branches.

**Outreach Program**

In 2024, Helen Nguyen coordinated a total of 32 outreach events across the Willoughby local government area. These events took the Library’s collections, staff expertise, and programs into shopping centres, parks, community halls, and neighbourhood houses, with the aim of meeting residents where they already gather. The annual report records that Helen Nguyen outreach_events_2024 is 32 events. Record status: historical. This figure represents an increase from the 27 outreach events delivered in 2023 and reflects the success of our efforts to expand the Library’s reach following the easing of restrictions in previous years.

The outreach calendar included a mix of regular monthly visits and one-off special events. The highlights of the year included:

- **Chatswood Mall Pop-Up Library** – A monthly stall offering borrowing, returns, and children’s activities. This averaged 45 visitors per session.
- **Willoughby Park Community Picnic** – A Library stall with craft activities and storytelling, attracting over 120 families.
- **Northbridge Plaza Seniors Morning** – A targeted session providing large-print materials, technology help, and library card sign-ups for older residents.
- **Artarmon Neighbourhood Centre Visits** – Quarterly visits offering book talks and collection requests for centre users.
- **Lane Cove River Festival** – A partnership stall promoting summer reading programs and environmental resources.

These events were supported by a roster of 14 staff members who volunteered their time outside their usual branch duties. The Library also received assistance from the Friends of the Library group at six of these events.

**Market Stalls and Community Information Sessions**

In addition to the outreach events led by Helen Nguyen, the Library participated in several community information sessions organised by Council. These included the Willoughby Seniors Expo in March, the Multicultural Community Forum in June, and the Youth Services Expo in September. At each of these sessions, Library staff provided information about membership, digital resources, and upcoming programs. A total of 380 individual enquiries were recorded across these three events.

**Mobile Library Service**

The Mobile Library continued to serve residents in areas without easy access to a branch. In 2024, the service operated on a fortnightly rotation of 12 stops, including the Castlecrag Village, the Willoughby Leisure Centre, and the High Street Shopping Village. The Mobile Library recorded 8,900 visits during the year, with an average of 28 items borrowed per stop per day. We were pleased to see a 12% increase in children’s borrowing from the Mobile Library, which we attribute to the addition of a dedicated picture book section introduced in February.

**Digital Outreach**

Recognising that not all community members can attend in-person events, we expanded our digital outreach offerings in 2024. This included a series of six “Library at Lunchtime” webinars, covering topics such as e-book basics, family history research, and online safety. The webinars were recorded and made available on the Library’s YouTube channel, where they have been viewed a combined 1,450 times. We also launched a monthly e-newsletter specifically for community partners, providing updates on Library services and upcoming events; this newsletter now has 230 subscribers.
**Collections and Resource Development**

The Library’s collection continued to grow in 2024, with a total of 312,450 items available across all branches and the Mobile Library. This represented a net increase of 4,850 items over the course of the year. The acquisitions budget of $486,000 was fully expended, allowing for the purchase of 18,300 new items, including books, e-books, audiobooks, DVDs, and magazines. We also received 1,150 items through donations, which were processed and added to the collection where they met our selection criteria.

The eBook and eAudio collection now comprises 68,400 titles, an increase of 9% on the previous year. Digital borrowing accounted for 23% of total circulation, up from 21% in 2023. The most popular digital titles of the year were the latest releases in the crime fiction and contemporary romance genres, reflecting broader reading trends reported by public libraries across New South Wales.

We continued to review the physical collection to ensure it remains relevant and in good condition. A total of 13,450 items were withdrawn during the year, either because they were damaged, superseded, or had not been borrowed in over two years. These items were offered to the Friends of the Library for their annual book sale, with the remainder recycled through the Council’s resource recovery program.

**Collection Highlights**

- The Local Studies collection was enhanced with the donation of a significant photographic archive documenting the development of the Willoughby area between 1950 and 1980. The collection has been digitised and is now available to view online through the Library’s catalogue.
- The Library acquired a new set of large-print titles specifically selected for older readers, with a focus on Australian authors and accessible formats.
- A targeted purchase of materials in Mandarin, Cantonese, Korean, and Italian was made in response to community feedback, increasing the multilingual collection by 1,200 items.

**Circulation and Membership**

Total circulation across all formats was 1,284,600 items, a decrease of 1.8% compared with 2023. While physical borrowing remained steady, digital circulation increased by 8%, which partially offset the decline in physical loans. The Library continues to monitor this trend and is adjusting the collection budget accordingly, with a greater proportion of funds directed towards digital resources in 2025.

Active membership at the end of December 2024 was 41,350, representing 52% of the Willoughby local government area population. This was an increase of 1,150 members on the previous year. New memberships were highest in the 0–5 years age group, reflecting the success of the Baby Bounce and Toddler Time programs, and among adults aged 25–34, many of whom joined to access the Library’s study spaces and digital resources.

**Staffing and Volunteers**

The Library ended the year with 68.5 full-time equivalent (FTE) staff, an increase of 1.5 FTE from 2023. The additional staffing was allocated to the Customer Service team at the Chatswood branch to manage increased opening hours introduced in February. Staff turnover was 11% for the year, slightly above the Council average, and we farewelled several long-serving team members, including our Children’s Services Librarian of 14 years, Margaret Chen, who retired in June.

Professional development remained a priority, with all library staff completing mandatory training in child safety, customer service, and emergency procedures. In addition, 12 staff members completed accredited training in digital literacy instruction, enabling them to deliver one-on-one technology help sessions. These sessions, introduced in March, have proven very popular, with 1,240 bookings taken over the year.
# Annual Report 2024–25
## Willoughby City Library Service

---

### Digital Services and Technology

The Library's digital platform continued to evolve throughout 2024, responding to changing patterns of community use and technological development. The online catalogue, library website, and mobile application were consolidated into a single integrated discovery layer in April, reducing the number of separate systems users needed to navigate from three to one. The new platform, branded *Willoughby Reads*, allows members to search the catalogue, manage their loans, book study rooms, and register for programs from a single login.

Usage of digital resources grew strongly during the year. E-book and e-audio loans totalled 214,300, an increase of 11% on 2023. The most popular e-book titles reflected a continuing appetite for crime fiction and contemporary Australian literature, while children's digital picture books, accessed primarily through the *StoryBox* platform, saw particularly strong growth following promotion through the Baby Bounce program.

Public computer usage at the Chatswood and Artarmon branches declined slightly, consistent with broader trends towards personal devices, but remained an essential service. The Library's 42 public access computers recorded 58,400 sessions over the year, with the highest demand observed on weekday afternoons and during school holidays. Free Wi-Fi sessions increased by 14% to 186,000 connections, and the Library upgraded its wireless infrastructure in October to support increased capacity and faster connection speeds.

A significant achievement in 2024 was the completion of the *Digital Skills for All* initiative, funded through a NSW State Library innovation grant. The program delivered 96 workshops across all branches, covering topics including basic computer use, internet safety, email, online banking, and the use of government services. A total of 1,180 residents participated, and post-program surveys indicated that 87% of participants felt more confident using digital technology. The program was delivered in partnership with the Willoughby Community College and the local Men's Shed, and several participants subsequently volunteered to assist with the Library's drop-in technology help sessions.

The one-on-one technology help sessions, introduced in March, continued to operate by appointment. Bookings reached 1,240 over the year, with demand consistently outstripping availability in the months following the program's launch. The Library is examining options to expand the service in 2025, including the possible recruitment of additional volunteer tutors to supplement the accredited staff who currently deliver the sessions.

---

### Heritage and Local Studies

The Local Studies collection at the Chatswood Library continued to serve as the primary repository for the history of the Willoughby local government area. During 2024, the collection received 412 research enquiries from the public, a slight increase on the previous year. Enquiries ranged from family history questions to requests from property owners seeking historical information about their homes, and from academic researchers examining the development of the North Shore region.

A major project completed during the year was the digitisation of the *Willoughby Advocate* newspaper for the period 1920–1949. This project, undertaken in partnership with the State Library of NSW's digital excellence program, resulted in 14,300 pages of historical newspapers being made freely available online through the National Library of Australia's *Trove* platform. The digitised issues were fully text-searchable, and usage statistics for the first six months following publication showed strong public engagement, with 28,500 page views recorded.
# Annual Report 2024

## Willoughby City Library

---

## Staff Recognition

The Library's success in 2024 was built on the commitment and professionalism of its staff. The Willoughby City Library team comprised 38 full-time equivalent staff members at year end, supported by a dedicated group of casual and part-time employees who provided essential coverage across all service points.

Several staff members reached significant service milestones during the year. Margaret Chen, Senior Librarian at the Chatswood Library, celebrated 25 years of service with Willoughby City Council. Margaret's leadership in the Local Studies area has been instrumental in building the collection into the respected community resource it is today. Robert Okafor, Library Technician, and Susan Park, Customer Service Officer, each completed 15 years of service.

The Library was pleased to support professional development throughout the year. Three staff members completed the Graduate Diploma in Information and Library Studies through Charles Sturt University, and two staff members presented at the annual conference of the Australian Library and Information Association. Staff participated in a range of training activities, including customer service excellence workshops, mental health first aid training, and cultural awareness sessions delivered in consultation with local Aboriginal community representatives.

In November, the Library hosted its annual Staff Excellence Awards. The 2024 award recipients were:

| Award | Recipient |
|-------|-----------|
| Excellence in Customer Service | James Whitfield, Chatswood Library |
| Innovation in Programming | Anita Desai, Northbridge Library |
| Community Engagement | Tom Gallagher, Outreach Services |
| Rising Star | Priya Raman, Mobile Library Service |

The Library also farewelled several long-serving staff members who retired during the year. David Thompson, who had served as the Library's Building and Facilities Coordinator since 2009, retired in March. His knowledge of the Library's physical infrastructure and his patient attention to maintenance matters are greatly missed. Helen Nguyen, Children's and Youth Services Librarian, retired in June after 22 years of service. Helen's creative storytelling programs and her warm relationships with generations of young library users leave a lasting legacy.

---

## Volunteers

Volunteers made an extraordinary contribution to Library services in 2024. A total of 87 active volunteers contributed 6,240 hours of service across the Library's branches and programs.

Volunteers supported the English Conversation Classes, the Home Library Service, the one-on-one technology help sessions, and the annual Summer Reading Club. They also assisted with shelving and shelf tidying at the Chatswood Library, freeing staff time for direct customer service. The Library's volunteer program continues to attract a diverse range of community members, including retirees, students, and recent migrants seeking to build local experience and connections.

The Library's Volunteer Recognition Afternoon was held on 12 December at the Chatswood Library. The event celebrated the contribution of all volunteers and featured the presentation of the Volunteer of the Year Award. The 2024 award was presented to Margaret O'Leary, who has volunteered with the Home Library Service since 2019. Margaret's reliability, warmth, and genuine care for the frail and isolated residents she visits have made her a much-valued member of the service.

**3. Collections and Circulation**

Our collections remain the core of our service. In 2023, we continued to focus on providing a diverse and current collection that reflects the interests and needs of our community.

- **Total Collection Size:** 318,450 items (physical and digital).
- **New Items Added:** 34,210 items were added to the collection, with a strong emphasis on new fiction, children's picture books, and non-fiction titles aligned with our community's interests.
- **Items Withdrawn:** 28,900 items were withdrawn from the collection due to condition or obsolescence, ensuring our shelves remain relevant and vibrant.
- **Total Circulation:** 1,245,780 items were borrowed or downloaded. This represents a 3.2% increase from the previous year.
- **Digital Circulation:** 245,600 e-books and e-audiobooks were borrowed, an 8.1% increase on 2022, reflecting the continued popularity of our digital platforms.

**4. Programs and Events**

The Library Service delivered a diverse and well-attended program of events and activities for all ages in 2023. A total of 1,480 programs were held across our branches, with a total attendance of 61,350.

**Children and Families**

Programs for children and families remain a key priority. Our regular storytime sessions, Baby Rhyme Time, and school holiday activities were consistently well attended. The **Summer Reading Challenge** (SRC), our flagship summer program, ran from December 2023 to the end of January 2024. The annual report states that Summer Reading Challenge participant_count_2023 is 1240 participants. Record status: historical. This figure is recorded as a historical count of registered participants for the 2023-24 challenge period. The Challenge encourages children to read a set number of books over the summer break, with incentives and a celebration event for those who complete the program. Feedback from parents and children was overwhelmingly positive, with many noting the program's success in fostering a love of reading during the long summer holidays.

- **Storytime & Baby Rhyme Time:** 480 sessions, with 14,200 attendees.
- **School Holiday Programs:** 120 sessions, with 4,500 attendees (including SRC events).
- **School Visits:** 85 class visits from local primary schools, reaching 2,100 students.

**Young Adults**

We have sought to provide a dedicated space and programs for our teen users. Our "Teen Zone" in the Chatswood branch has become a popular after-school hub.

- **Teen Book Club:** Monthly meetings with an average attendance of 12 participants.
- **Game On! Sessions:** Fortnightly video game and board game sessions in the Teen Zone, with an average of 20 attendees per session.
- **Homework Help:** A volunteer-led tutoring service, offered four afternoons per week during the school term, assisted 580 students.

**Adults and Seniors**

Our adult programs have focused on lifelong learning, digital literacy, and social connection.

- **Author Talks and Book Launches:** 25 events, with a total attendance of 1,150.
- **Digital Help Drop-in Sessions:** Weekly one-on-one sessions to assist with technology, from using a smartphone to setting up email, attended by 720 people.
- **Book Clubs:** We host and support 14 community book clubs, with over 150 members.
- **Seniors' Morning Tea:** A monthly social gathering, with an average attendance of 35 people.
- **ESL Conversation Classes:** Weekly classes run in partnership with the Willoughby Community College, with an average of 18 attendees per session.

**Community Partnerships and Volunteers**

The Library’s work would not be possible without the strong network of community partners and volunteers who support our programs and services throughout the year. We are fortunate to work alongside a range of local organisations, schools, and community groups who share our commitment to fostering literacy, learning, and connection in Willoughby.

**Wattlebridge Library Friends**

The Wattlebridge Library Friends continue to be one of our most valued partners, providing financial support for programs and resources that fall outside the core Library budget. Their fundraising efforts throughout the year enabled us to purchase new furniture for the Teen Zone, fund the Summer Reading Challenge prize pool, and support the author talk series.

The historical records indicate that Wattlebridge Library Friends founding_year is 1998. Record status: historical. This founding year places the group among the longer-standing volunteer support organisations in the local area, and we are grateful for the quarter-century of service they have provided to the Library and the wider community. Over the past year, the Friends have contributed 1,850 volunteer hours, and their membership has grown to 65 active members. We extend our sincere thanks to the Friends’ committee, led by President Margaret Chen, for their dedication and enthusiasm.

**Local Schools and Early Childhood Centres**

Our partnerships with local schools remain a cornerstone of our outreach work. In addition to the class visits noted earlier in this report, we collaborated with Chatswood Public School and Northbridge Public School on a joint reading program for Year 3 and Year 4 students. The program, running over eight weeks, paired students with Library staff for guided reading sessions and culminated in a visit to the Library for a storytelling event. A total of 14 classes participated, involving 320 students.

We also worked with three local early childhood centres to deliver a series of “First Five Forever” sessions for parents and carers. These sessions, funded by the State Library of Queensland, focused on early literacy skills and were attended by 90 families.

**Community Organisations and Service Clubs**

The Library continued its partnership with the Willoughby Community College to deliver ESL Conversation Classes, which have proven to be a vital resource for new migrants and refugees. The weekly classes, held on Tuesday mornings, maintain an average attendance of 18 participants. We also welcomed the Rotary Club of Chatswood as a new partner in 2023, working together to establish a “Little Free Library” at the Chatswood Mall. The initiative has been well received, with over 400 books exchanged in its first six months of operation.

Our relationship with the Chatswood Chamber of Commerce has also deepened this year. The Chamber sponsored our “Local Authors Showcase” event in October, which featured six local writers and attracted an audience of 180 people. The event provided a platform for emerging voices and strengthened the Library’s connection with the local creative community.

**Volunteers**

Volunteers are integral to the daily operations of the Library. In 2023, we were supported by 142 active volunteers who contributed a total of 6,300 hours across all branches. Their roles included:

We are grateful for the generosity and commitment of all our volunteers, whose contributions help us deliver a wide range of services to the community. In recognition of their efforts, we held our annual Volunteer Appreciation Morning Tea in November, which was attended by 85 volunteers and staff members.

**Community Engagement**

The Library’s community engagement work in 2024 focused on deepening existing partnerships, reaching new audiences, and ensuring that our programs reflect the diversity of the communities we serve. This work is led by our Community Engagement Officer, Helen Nguyen, whose efforts have been central to the Library’s growing presence beyond our physical branches.

**Outreach Program**

In 2024, Helen Nguyen coordinated a total of 32 outreach events across the Willoughby local government area. These events took the Library’s collections, staff expertise, and programs into shopping centres, parks, community halls, and neighbourhood houses, with the aim of meeting residents where they already gather. The annual report records that Helen Nguyen outreach_events_2024 is 32 events. Record status: historical. This figure represents an increase from the 27 outreach events delivered in 2023 and reflects the success of our efforts to expand the Library’s reach following the easing of restrictions in previous years.

The outreach calendar included a mix of regular monthly visits and one-off special events. The highlights of the year included:

- **Chatswood Mall Pop-Up Library** – A monthly stall offering borrowing, returns, and children’s activities. This averaged 45 visitors per session.
- **Willoughby Park Community Picnic** – A Library stall with craft activities and storytelling, attracting over 120 families.
- **Northbridge Plaza Seniors Morning** – A targeted session providing large-print materials, technology help, and library card sign-ups for older residents.
- **Artarmon Neighbourhood Centre Visits** – Quarterly visits offering book talks and collection requests for centre users.
- **Lane Cove River Festival** – A partnership stall promoting summer reading programs and environmental resources.

These events were supported by a roster of 14 staff members who volunteered their time outside their usual branch duties. The Library also received assistance from the Friends of the Library group at six of these events.

**Market Stalls and Community Information Sessions**

In addition to the outreach events led by Helen Nguyen, the Library participated in several community information sessions organised by Council. These included the Willoughby Seniors Expo in March, the Multicultural Community Forum in June, and the Youth Services Expo in September. At each of these sessions, Library staff provided information about membership, digital resources, and upcoming programs. A total of 380 individual enquiries were recorded across these three events.

**Mobile Library Service**

The Mobile Library continued to serve residents in areas without easy access to a branch. In 2024, the service operated on a fortnightly rotation of 12 stops, including the Castlecrag Village, the Willoughby Leisure Centre, and the High Street Shopping Village. The Mobile Library recorded 8,900 visits during the year, with an average of 28 items borrowed per stop per day. We were pleased to see a 12% increase in children’s borrowing from the Mobile Library, which we attribute to the addition of a dedicated picture book section introduced in February.

**Digital Outreach**

Recognising that not all community members can attend in-person events, we expanded our digital outreach offerings in 2024. This included a series of six “Library at Lunchtime” webinars, covering topics such as e-book basics, family history research, and online safety. The webinars were recorded and made available on the Library’s YouTube channel, where they have been viewed a combined 1,450 times. We also launched a monthly e-newsletter specifically for community partners, providing updates on Library services and upcoming events; this newsletter now has 230 subscribers.

**Collections and Resource Development**

The Library’s collection continued to grow in 2024, with a total of 312,450 items available across all branches and the Mobile Library. This represented a net increase of 4,850 items over the course of the year. The acquisitions budget of $486,000 was fully expended, allowing for the purchase of 18,300 new items, including books, e-books, audiobooks, DVDs, and magazines. We also received 1,150 items through donations, which were processed and added to the collection where they met our selection criteria.

The eBook and eAudio collection now comprises 68,400 titles, an increase of 9% on the previous year. Digital borrowing accounted for 23% of total circulation, up from 21% in 2023. The most popular digital titles of the year were the latest releases in the crime fiction and contemporary romance genres, reflecting broader reading trends reported by public libraries across New South Wales.

We continued to review the physical collection to ensure it remains relevant and in good condition. A total of 13,450 items were withdrawn during the year, either because they were damaged, superseded, or had not been borrowed in over two years. These items were offered to the Friends of the Library for their annual book sale, with the remainder recycled through the Council’s resource recovery program.

**Collection Highlights**

- The Local Studies collection was enhanced with the donation of a significant photographic archive documenting the development of the Willoughby area between 1950 and 1980. The collection has been digitised and is now available to view online through the Library’s catalogue.
- The Library acquired a new set of large-print titles specifically selected for older readers, with a focus on Australian authors and accessible formats.
- A targeted purchase of materials in Mandarin, Cantonese, Korean, and Italian was made in response to community feedback, increasing the multilingual collection by 1,200 items.

**Circulation and Membership**

Total circulation across all formats was 1,284,600 items, a decrease of 1.8% compared with 2023. While physical borrowing remained steady, digital circulation increased by 8%, which partially offset the decline in physical loans. The Library continues to monitor this trend and is adjusting the collection budget accordingly, with a greater proportion of funds directed towards digital resources in 2025.

Active membership at the end of December 2024 was 41,350, representing 52% of the Willoughby local government area population. This was an increase of 1,150 members on the previous year. New memberships were highest in the 0–5 years age group, reflecting the success of the Baby Bounce and Toddler Time programs, and among adults aged 25–34, many of whom joined to access the Library’s study spaces and digital resources.

**Staffing and Volunteers**

The Library ended the year with 68.5 full-time equivalent (FTE) staff, an increase of 1.5 FTE from 2023. The additional staffing was allocated to the Customer Service team at the Chatswood branch to manage increased opening hours introduced in February. Staff turnover was 11% for the year, slightly above the Council average, and we farewelled several long-serving team members, including our Children’s Services Librarian of 14 years, Margaret Chen, who retired in June.

Professional development remained a priority, with all library staff completing mandatory training in child safety, customer service, and emergency procedures. In addition, 12 staff members completed accredited training in digital literacy instruction, enabling them to deliver one-on-one technology help sessions. These sessions, introduced in March, have proven very popular, with 1,240 bookings taken over the year.

# Annual Report 2024–25
## Willoughby City Library Service

---

### Digital Services and Technology

The Library's digital platform continued to evolve throughout 2024, responding to changing patterns of community use and technological development. The online catalogue, library website, and mobile application were consolidated into a single integrated discovery layer in April, reducing the number of separate systems users needed to navigate from three to one. The new platform, branded *Willoughby Reads*, allows members to search the catalogue, manage their loans, book study rooms, and register for programs from a single login.

Usage of digital resources grew strongly during the year. E-book and e-audio loans totalled 214,300, an increase of 11% on 2023. The most popular e-book titles reflected a continuing appetite for crime fiction and contemporary Australian literature, while children's digital picture books, accessed primarily through the *StoryBox* platform, saw particularly strong growth following promotion through the Baby Bounce program.

Public computer usage at the Chatswood and Artarmon branches declined slightly, consistent with broader trends towards personal devices, but remained an essential service. The Library's 42 public access computers recorded 58,400 sessions over the year, with the highest demand observed on weekday afternoons and during school holidays. Free Wi-Fi sessions increased by 14% to 186,000 connections, and the Library upgraded its wireless infrastructure in October to support increased capacity and faster connection speeds.

A significant achievement in 2024 was the completion of the *Digital Skills for All* initiative, funded through a NSW State Library innovation grant. The program delivered 96 workshops across all branches, covering topics including basic computer use, internet safety, email, online banking, and the use of government services. A total of 1,180 residents participated, and post-program surveys indicated that 87% of participants felt more confident using digital technology. The program was delivered in partnership with the Willoughby Community College and the local Men's Shed, and several participants subsequently volunteered to assist with the Library's drop-in technology help sessions.

The one-on-one technology help sessions, introduced in March, continued to operate by appointment. Bookings reached 1,240 over the year, with demand consistently outstripping availability in the months following the program's launch. The Library is examining options to expand the service in 2025, including the possible recruitment of additional volunteer tutors to supplement the accredited staff who currently deliver the sessions.

---

### Heritage and Local Studies

The Local Studies collection at the Chatswood Library continued to serve as the primary repository for the history of the Willoughby local government area. During 2024, the collection received 412 research enquiries from the public, a slight increase on the previous year. Enquiries ranged from family history questions to requests from property owners seeking historical information about their homes, and from academic researchers examining the development of the North Shore region.

A major project completed during the year was the digitisation of the *Willoughby Advocate* newspaper for the period 1920–1949. This project, undertaken in partnership with the State Library of NSW's digital excellence program, resulted in 14,300 pages of historical newspapers being made freely available online through the National Library of Australia's *Trove* platform. The digitised issues were fully text-searchable, and usage statistics for the first six months following publication showed strong public engagement, with 28,500 page views recorded.

# Annual Report 2024

## Willoughby City Library

---

## Staff Recognition

The Library's success in 2024 was built on the commitment and professionalism of its staff. The Willoughby City Library team comprised 38 full-time equivalent staff members at year end, supported by a dedicated group of casual and part-time employees who provided essential coverage across all service points.

Several staff members reached significant service milestones during the year. Margaret Chen, Senior Librarian at the Chatswood Library, celebrated 25 years of service with Willoughby City Council. Margaret's leadership in the Local Studies area has been instrumental in building the collection into the respected community resource it is today. Robert Okafor, Library Technician, and Susan Park, Customer Service Officer, each completed 15 years of service.

The Library was pleased to support professional development throughout the year. Three staff members completed the Graduate Diploma in Information and Library Studies through Charles Sturt University, and two staff members presented at the annual conference of the Australian Library and Information Association. Staff participated in a range of training activities, including customer service excellence workshops, mental health first aid training, and cultural awareness sessions delivered in consultation with local Aboriginal community representatives.

In November, the Library hosted its annual Staff Excellence Awards. The 2024 award recipients were:

| Award | Recipient |
|-------|-----------|
| Excellence in Customer Service | James Whitfield, Chatswood Library |
| Innovation in Programming | Anita Desai, Northbridge Library |
| Community Engagement | Tom Gallagher, Outreach Services |
| Rising Star | Priya Raman, Mobile Library Service |

The Library also farewelled several long-serving staff members who retired during the year. David Thompson, who had served as the Library's Building and Facilities Coordinator since 2009, retired in March. His knowledge of the Library's physical infrastructure and his patient attention to maintenance matters are greatly missed. Helen Nguyen, Children's and Youth Services Librarian, retired in June after 22 years of service. Helen's creative storytelling programs and her warm relationships with generations of young library users leave a lasting legacy.

---

## Volunteers

Volunteers made an extraordinary contribution to Library services in 2024. A total of 87 active volunteers contributed 6,240 hours of service across the Library's branches and programs.

Volunteers supported the English Conversation Classes, the Home Library Service, the one-on-one technology help sessions, and the annual Summer Reading Club. They also assisted with shelving and shelf tidying at the Chatswood Library, freeing staff time for direct customer service. The Library's volunteer program continues to attract a diverse range of community members, including retirees, students, and recent migrants seeking to build local experience and connections.

The Library's Volunteer Recognition Afternoon was held on 12 December at the Chatswood Library. The event celebrated the contribution of all volunteers and featured the presentation of the Volunteer of the Year Award. The 2024 award was presented to Margaret O'Leary, who has volunteered with the Home Library Service since 2019. Margaret's reliability, warmth, and genuine care for the frail and isolated residents she visits have made her a much-valued member of the service.
